claim: The Ya Tsie trial was conducted from 2013 to 2018 in 30 rural and peri-urban communities in Botswana.
source: The Ya Tsie trial or Botswana Combination Prevention Project (BCPP) was a pair-matched community randomized trial to evaluate whether an optimized combination of effective HIV treatment and prevention interventions would substantially reduce population-level HIV incidence over 29 months. The trial was conducted from 2013 to 2018 in 30 rural and peri-urban communities (average population size: 5855) in the Central, South-East, and North/North-East regions of Botswana that represented an estimated total population of 175,664 (7.6% of the national population) (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the trial period and number of communities.

claim: The average population size of trial communities was 5,855.
source: The trial was conducted from 2013 to 2018 in 30 rural and peri-urban communities (average population size: 5855) in the Central, South-East, and North/North-East regions of Botswana that represented an estimated total population of 175,664 (7.6% of the national population) (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides the average population size of trial communities.

claim: The trial represented an estimated total population of 175,664, which is 7.6% of Botswana's national population.
source: The trial was conducted from 2013 to 2018 in 30 rural and peri-urban communities (average population size: 5855) in the Central, South-East, and North/North-East regions of Botswana that represented an estimated total population of 175,664 (7.6% of the national population) (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides the total population represented by the trial and its percentage of the national population.

claim: 13,131 adults aged 16–64 years gave informed consent to participate in the trial.
source: Among eligible community residents, 13,131 adults aged 16–64 years gave informed consent to participate in the trial.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of participants who consented.

claim: The estimated HIV prevalence among participating communities at the start of the trial was 25.7%.
source: The estimated HIV prevalence among participating communities at the start of the trial was 25.7% (27,446 / 106,712) (Supplementary file 1-Table 1A) (see Materials and methods section on computing age-gender estimates of the number of people with HIV in each trial community).
evidence: The manuscript provides the estimated HIV prevalence at baseline.

claim: Communities were matched into 15 pairs according to population size and age structure, access to health services, and geographic location relative to major urban centers.
source: Communities were matched into 15 pairs according to population size and age structure, access to health services, and geographic location relative to major urban centers; communities in each pair were then randomized into intervention and control arms.
evidence: The manuscript describes the matching criteria for community pairs.

claim: Intervention communities received expanded HIV testing, early initiation of antiretroviral treatment, and strengthened linkage-to-care.
source: Intervention communities received expanded HIV testing, early initiation of antiretroviral treatment, and strengthened linkage-to-care, for example, clinic referrals with appointment dates, text alert reminders of appointments, and following-up with those who missed appointments.
evidence: The manuscript describes the intervention package provided to intervention communities.

claim: Botswana is roughly the size of France at 581,730 km² (224,610 square miles).
source: Botswana is a sparsely populated, landlocked country in southern Africa, roughly the size of France, 581,730 km2 (224,610 square miles), with a population of about 2.3 million people.
evidence: The manuscript provides the geographic size of Botswana.

claim: Botswana has a population of about 2.3 million people.
source: Botswana is a sparsely populated, landlocked country in southern Africa, roughly the size of France, 581,730 km2 (224,610 square miles), with a population of about 2.3 million people.
evidence: The manuscript provides the population size of Botswana.

claim: The Kalahari Desert occupies approximately 70% of Botswana.
source: The Kalahari Desert occupies approximately 70% of the country, and the population is largely distributed along an eastern corridor bordered by South Africa, Zambia, and Zimbabwe (GISGeography, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites a source for the geographic distribution of Botswana.

claim: Botswana is a high middle-income country with a Gini index of 53.3.
source: It is a high middle-income country with a Gini index of 53.3 (The World Bank, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites World Bank data for Botswana's economic status and inequality measure.

claim: One in five adults in Botswana aged 15–49 years were reported to be living with HIV in 2019.
source: One in five adults in Botswana aged 15–49 years were reported to be living with HIV in 2019, representing the third-highest HIV prevalence in the world after Lesotho and Eswatini (UNAIDS, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites UNAIDS data for HIV prevalence in Botswana.

claim: Botswana had the third-highest HIV prevalence in the world in 2019 after Lesotho and Eswatini.
source: One in five adults in Botswana aged 15–49 years were reported to be living with HIV in 2019, representing the third-highest HIV prevalence in the world after Lesotho and Eswatini (UNAIDS, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites UNAIDS data for global HIV prevalence rankings.

claim: 5,114 trial participants consented to viral genotyping and their viral genomes were successfully deep-sequenced.
source: Altogether, 5114 participants consented to a blood draw for HIV-1 viral genotyping and their viral genomes were successfully deep-sequenced, representing the largest phylogenetics study conducted in Botswana (Supplementary file 1-Table 1A).
evidence: The manuscript provides the number of participants with successful viral sequencing.

claim: This represents the largest phylogenetics study conducted in Botswana.
source: Altogether, 5114 participants consented to a blood draw for HIV-1 viral genotyping and their viral genomes were successfully deep-sequenced, representing the largest phylogenetics study conducted in Botswana (Supplementary file 1-Table 1A).
evidence: The manuscript claims this is the largest phylogenetics study in Botswana.

claim: Most inferred HIV transmissions within the trial occurred within the same or between neighboring communities.
source: Deep-sequence phylogenetic analysis revealed that most inferred HIV transmissions within the trial occurred within the same or between neighboring communities, and between similarly aged partners.
evidence: The abstract summarizes a key finding from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Most inferred HIV transmissions occurred between similarly aged partners.
source: Deep-sequence phylogenetic analysis revealed that most inferred HIV transmissions within the trial occurred within the same or between neighboring communities, and between similarly aged partners.
evidence: The abstract summarizes a key finding about age patterns in transmission.

claim: Transmissions into intervention communities from control communities were more common than the reverse post-baseline (30% vs. 3%).
source: Transmissions into intervention communities from control communities were more common than the reverse post-baseline (30% [12.2 – 56.7] vs. 3% [0.1 – 27.3]) than at baseline (7% [1.5 – 25.3] vs. 5% [0.9 – 22.9]) compatible with a benefit from treatment-as-prevention.
evidence: The abstract provides estimates with confidence intervals for transmission flows between trial arms.

claim: At baseline, transmissions into intervention communities from control communities were 7% compared to 5% in the reverse direction.
source: Transmissions into intervention communities from control communities were more common than the reverse post-baseline (30% [12.2 – 56.7] vs. 3% [0.1 – 27.3]) than at baseline (7% [1.5 – 25.3] vs. 5% [0.9 – 22.9]) compatible with a benefit from treatment-as-prevention.
evidence: The abstract provides baseline estimates with confidence intervals for transmission flows.

claim: The pattern of transmissions between trial arms is compatible with a benefit from treatment-as-prevention.
source: Transmissions into intervention communities from control communities were more common than the reverse post-baseline (30% [12.2 – 56.7] vs. 3% [0.1 – 27.3]) than at baseline (7% [1.5 – 25.3] vs. 5% [0.9 – 22.9]) compatible with a benefit from treatment-as-prevention.
evidence: The abstract interprets the transmission patterns as consistent with intervention benefit.

claim: Population mobility patterns are fundamental to HIV transmission dynamics and to the impact of HIV control strategies.
source: Our findings suggest that population mobility patterns are fundamental to HIV transmission dynamics and to the impact of HIV control strategies.
evidence: The abstract concludes with an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The global number of new HIV-1 infections has gradually declined since the peak in 1997.
source: The global number of new infections with HIV-1, the virus that causes AIDS, has gradually declined since the peak in 1997, yet population-level HIV incidence remains high in East and Southern Africa, especially among young women (UNAIDS, 2019; UNAIDS, 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites UNAIDS reports for global HIV trends.

claim: Population-level HIV incidence remains high in East and Southern Africa, especially among young women.
source: The global number of new infections with HIV-1, the virus that causes AIDS, has gradually declined since the peak in 1997, yet population-level HIV incidence remains high in East and Southern Africa, especially among young women (UNAIDS, 2019; UNAIDS, 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites UNAIDS reports for regional HIV trends.

claim: There is still no successful HIV vaccine or widely administrable cure after four decades of efforts.
source: Despite efforts spanning four decades, there is still no successful HIV vaccine or widely administrable cure.
evidence: The introduction states the current status of HIV vaccine and cure development.

claim: Four large cluster-randomized trials were recently conducted in East and Southern Africa to evaluate universal HIV testing and treatment.
source: Four large cluster-randomized trials were recently conducted in East (Kenya and Uganda) and Southern Africa (Botswana, South Africa, and Zambia) to evaluate the effect of universal HIV testing and treatment in reducing population-level HIV incidence (Hayes et al., 2019; Makhema et al., 2019; Havlir et al., 2019; Iwuji et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple trial publications.

claim: The universal test-and-treat trials showed variable outcomes, ranging from modest to no reduction in new HIV infections.
source: The trials showed variable outcomes, ranging from modest to no reduction in the occurrence of new HIV infections (Abdool Karim, 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites a review of trial outcomes.

claim: Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy substantially reduced onward transmission in people with HIV owing to suppressed virus levels.
source: The trials were motivated by evidence that early initiation of antiretroviral therapy substantially reduced onward transmission in people with HIV owing to suppressed virus levels (Cohen et al., 2016) and by mathematical models predicting that widely expanded access to HIV testing and treatment would rapidly and substantially reduce the occurrence of new infections (Granich et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites evidence for treatment-as-prevention.

claim: Mathematical models predicted that widely expanded access to HIV testing and treatment would rapidly and substantially reduce new infections.
source: The trials were motivated by evidence that early initiation of antiretroviral therapy substantially reduced onward transmission in people with HIV owing to suppressed virus levels (Cohen et al., 2016) and by mathematical models predicting that widely expanded access to HIV testing and treatment would rapidly and substantially reduce the occurrence of new infections (Granich et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites mathematical modeling predictions.

claim: UNAIDS had set a global target of fewer than 500,000 new HIV infections by 2020 that was unmet.
source: The joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) had set a global target of fewer than 500,000 new HIV infections by 2020 that was unmet.
evidence: The introduction states a UNAIDS target and its outcome.

claim: Previous work in Kwa-Zulu Natal, South Africa identified age-disparate sexual partnerships between younger women under 25 years and older men as a primary contributor to HIV transmission.
source: Previous work in a high HIV burden setting in Kwa-Zulu Natal, South Africa identified age-disparate sexual partnerships between younger women under 25 years and older men as a primary contributor to HIV transmission and incidence in younger women (de Oliveira et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites previous phylogenetic work on age-disparate partnerships.

claim: Most participants with HIV at time of enrollment were on antiretroviral treatment and virally suppressed (86%).
source: At the time of identification, most (86%, n = 4410) individuals with HIV-1 infection were on antiretroviral therapy and virally suppressed (≤400 copies per ml of blood plasma).
evidence: The results section provides data on treatment and viral suppression status.

claim: Deep-sequencing of HIV viral genomes was generally done on proviral DNA (81%).
source: Because most participants were virally suppressed at the time of sampling, deep sequencing of HIV-1 viral genomes was generally done on proviral DNA (81%, n = 4142) (Novitsky et al., 2015) (see Materials and methods section on paired-end deep-sequencing of HIV viral genomes for phylogenetic analyses).
evidence: The results section provides data on the source material for sequencing.

claim: 3,832 participants met minimum criteria for inclusion in phylogenetic analyses.
source: Our analysis was restricted to samples from 3832 participants (approximately 14% of the estimated 27,446 individuals living with HIV in trial communities) who had available demographic information and met minimum criteria on genome missingness (≥6300 nucleotides available) for inclusion in phylogenetic analyses.
evidence: The methods section specifies the number of participants meeting inclusion criteria.

claim: The overall genotyping density across all 30 trial communities was 14%.
source: Sampling (or genotyping) density is defined as the estimated proportion of individuals living with HIV in a trial community that were included in our sample. Intervention communities were sampled more densely, 16% (2281 / 14,263) than control communities, 12% (1551 / 13,183); and sampling densities among all 30 trial communities ranged from 2.7% to 36.2% (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1, Table 1C) (see Materials and methods section on computing age-gender estimates of the number of people with HIV in each trial community).
evidence: The methods section provides sampling density data.

claim: Intervention communities were sampled more densely (16%) than control communities (12%).
source: Intervention communities were sampled more densely, 16% (2281 / 14,263) than control communities, 12% (1551 / 13,183); and sampling densities among all 30 trial communities ranged from 2.7% to 36.2% (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1, Table 1C) (see Materials and methods section on computing age-gender estimates of the number of people with HIV in each trial community).
evidence: The methods section provides differential sampling density by trial arm.

claim: The mean pairwise genetic distance between HIV-1 viral whole-genome consensus sequences was 12.5 ± 3.0%.
source: The mean ± standard deviation pairwise genetic distance between HIV-1 viral whole-genome consensus sequences of participants included in phylogenetic analyses was 12.5 ± 3.0%, and the maximum pairwise distance was 40% substitutions per site (Figure 3A) (see Materials and methods on comparing genetic distances between HIV-1 viral consensus sequences of trial participants included in phylogenetic analyses).
evidence: The results section provides genetic distance statistics.

claim: 236 genetic similarity clusters were identified comprising HIV-1 viral consensus sequences from 14% (525 / 3832) of the participants.
source: We identified 236 genetic similarity clusters comprising HIV-1 viral consensus sequences from 14% (525 / 3832) of the participants (Figure 5) (see Materials and methods section on consensus sequence phylogenetics to identify clusters of participants with genetically similar HIV-1 infections).
evidence: The results section provides data on genetic clustering.

claim: 97% (230 / 236) of genetic clusters comprised two or three members.
source: The sizes of genetic clusters ranged from 2 to 12 members, with 97% (230 / 236) of clusters comprising two or three members (Figure 6).
evidence: The results section provides data on cluster size distribution.

claim: 52% (124 / 236) of the clusters were entirely within a single community.
source: Overall, however, genetic clusters were generally concentrated within geographic regions (Central-East, North/North-East, and South-East) than spread out across them (Figure 5), with 42% (100 / 236) of clusters localized to two communities (Figure 7) and 52% (124 / 236) of the clusters entirely within a single community (Figure 7).
evidence: The results section provides data on geographic distribution of clusters.

claim: 153 highly supported probable source-recipient pairs were identified within 236 clusters of genetically similar HIV-1 infections.
source: We identified 153 highly supported probable source-recipient pairs within 236 clusters of genetically similar HIV-1 infections. Seventy-one were same-sex linkages between women (n = 65) or men (n = 6), and the remaining were male-female pairs (n = 82).
evidence: The results section provides data on identified transmission pairs.

claim: 82 male-female probable transmission pairs were identified.
source: We identified 153 highly supported probable source-recipient pairs within 236 clusters of genetically similar HIV-1 infections. Seventy-one were same-sex linkages between women (n = 65) or men (n = 6), and the remaining were male-female pairs (n = 82).
evidence: The results section provides data on male-female transmission pairs.

claim: The estimated false discovery rate for inferring direct transmission between males and females in phylogenetically linked male-female pairs was 36%.
source: We used the probability of inferring a phylogenetically linked directed male-male pair in the sample to calibrate an upper bound on the FDR of inferring direct transmission between males and females in phylogenetically linked male-female pairs; the estimated number of linked male-female pairs in the sample with unsampled intermediates was approximately 30, corresponding to a FDR of 36% (30 / 82) (see Materials and methods section on estimating error rates in phylogenetic inference of direct transmission between sampled males and females).
evidence: The results section provides an estimated false discovery rate.

claim: Males were a mean ± standard deviation of 3.5 ± 9.6 years older than females in probable transmission pairs overall.
source: Males were a mean ± standard deviation of 3.5 ± 9.6 years older than females in probable transmission pairs overall, with a difference of 4.9 ± 7.5 in male-to-female transmission events, and 1.8 ± 11.6 years in female-to-male transmission events.
evidence: The results section provides age difference statistics.

claim: 55% of the 82 inferred male-female transmission events originated from men.
source: 55% [95% CI: 39.8 – 69.1] of the 82 inferred male-female transmission events originated from men with the remainder occurring from women, 45% [30.9 – 60.2] (Figure 13).
evidence: The results section provides data on the direction of transmission by gender.

claim: 69% (57 / 82) of the sampled transmission events occurred within the same trial community.
source: The proportion of inferred transmission events of HIV-1 infection in the deep-sequenced sample between members of the same trial community was 69% (57 / 82) compared with 21% (17 / 82) for members of different trial communities in the same region, and 10% (8 / 82) for members of trial communities in different regions (Figures 13 and 14).
evidence: The results section provides data on geographic distribution of transmission events.

claim: The median driving distance between trial communities for transmission pairs was 161 km [108 – 420 km].
source: For pairs where transmission events linked people in different trial communities the median [lower–upper quartile] driving distance between the trial communities was 161 km [108 – 420 km] or 100 mi [67 – 261 mi] and the median drive time was 1.86 hr [1.41 – 4.68 hr].
evidence: The results section provides data on geographic distances between communities with transmission links.

claim: After adjusting for differential sampling by community, an estimated 24% of transmissions to a resident of a trial community originated from another trial community.
source: After adjusting for differential sampling by community, an estimated 24% of transmissions to a resident of a trial community originated from another trial community (Supplementary file 1-Table 1I) (see Materials and methods section on adjustment for variable sampling rates across different demographic groups or randomized-HIV-interventions).
evidence: The results section provides adjusted estimates of between-community transmission.

claim: The estimated proportion of HIV transmissions in the trial population within the South-East region (50%) was higher compared to the Central-East (23%) and North-East regions (18%).
source: The estimated proportion of HIV transmissions in the trial population, after adjusting for differential sampling by geographic region, that occurred within the South-East region, 50% [95% CI: 29.6 – 70.5] was higher compared to that in the Central-East, 23% [9.7 – 45.4] and North-East regions, 18% [6.5 – 39.8], respectively (Figure 15A and Supplementary file 1-Table 1J) (see Materials and methods section on adjustment for variable sampling rates across different demographic groups or randomized-HIV-interventions).
evidence: The results section provides adjusted estimates of transmission by geographic region.

claim: 79% (65 / 82) of inferred transmission events occurred within intervention or within control communities.
source: The proportion of inferred transmission events of HIV-1 infection in the deep-sequenced sample occurring within intervention (n = 33) or within control communities (n = 32) was 79% (65 / 82) compared with 21% (17 / 82) across intervention and control communities (Figures 13 and 14).
evidence: The results section provides data on transmission patterns by trial arm.

claim: There were more transmission events identified in intervention communities that originated from control communities than the reverse (n = 13 vs. 4).
source: There were more transmission events identified in intervention communities that originated from control communities than the reverse (n = 13 vs. 4).
evidence: The results section provides data on directional transmission between trial arms.

claim: After adjusting for differential sampling by trial arm, the estimated proportion of HIV transmissions within control communities (51%) was about twice that in intervention communities (29%).
source: After adjusting for differential sampling by trial arm, the estimated proportions of HIV transmissions in the trial population within control communities, 51% [35.9 – 66.5] was about twice that predicted in intervention communities, 29% [16.6 – 44.6] (Figure 15B and Supplementary file 1-Table 1K); and the estimated proportion of HIV transmissions in the trial population flowing into intervention communities from control communities, 15% [6.9 – 30.1] was about three times higher than the reverse, 5% [1.0 – 16.9] (see Materials and methods section on adjustment for variable sampling rates across different demographic groups or randomized-HIV-interventions).
evidence: The results section provides adjusted estimates of transmission within trial arms.

claim: The estimated proportion of HIV transmissions flowing into intervention communities from control communities (15%) was about three times higher than the reverse (5%).
source: After adjusting for differential sampling by trial arm, the estimated proportions of HIV transmissions in the trial population within control communities, 51% [35.9 – 66.5] was about twice that predicted in intervention communities, 29% [16.6 – 44.6] (Figure 15B and Supplementary file 1-Table 1K); and the estimated proportion of HIV transmissions in the trial population flowing into intervention communities from control communities, 15% [6.9 – 30.1] was about three times higher than the reverse, 5% [1.0 – 16.9] (see Materials and methods section on adjustment for variable sampling rates across different demographic groups or randomized-HIV-interventions).
evidence: The results section provides adjusted estimates of transmission between trial arms.

claim: Men and women for whom sexual partners could be inferred phylogenetically contributed similarly to viral transmission of HIV-1 infection in the trial.
source: Following an adjustment for variable sampling by age and gender (Figure 12), we found that men and women for whom sexual partners could be inferred phylogenetically contributed similarly to viral transmission of HIV-1 infection in the Botswana/Ya Tsie trial (see Materials and methods section on adjustment for variable sampling rates across different demographic groups or randomized-HIV-interventions).
evidence: The discussion section interprets adjusted results on gender contribution to transmission.

claim: There was little genetic evidence to suggest that older men were a substantial source of HIV-1 infection to younger women in Botswana.
source: In the phylogenetic analyses of the Botswana/Ya Tsie study, there was little genetic evidence from analyses of deep-sequence data to suggest that older men were a substantial source of HIV-1 infection to younger women in Botswana.
evidence: The discussion section interprets the findings on age-disparate transmission.

claim: The VOICE trial found no association between age-disparate relationships and risk of HIV-1 infection in young women under 25 years in South Africa.
source: Consistent with our results, the Vaginal and Oral Interventions to Control the Epidemic (VOICE) trial, a placebo-controlled randomized study of pre-exposure prophylaxis to test the efficacy of providing oral and vaginal gel tenofovir to women in Southern Africa to prevent HIV infection (Saag, 2015; Balkus et al., 2015), found no association between age-disparate relationships and risk of HIV-1 infection in young women under 25 years residing in South Africa in the cities of Durban, Johannesburg, and Klerksdorp who had male partners that were >5 years older at enrollment.
evidence: The discussion section cites another study with consistent findings.

claim: Participants with genetically similar HIV-1 infections tended to aggregate in small-sized (two- or three-person) clusters.
source: Participants with genetically similar HIV-1 infections in the Botswana/Ya Tsie trial tended to aggregate in small-sized (two- or three-person) clusters.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes a key finding about cluster sizes.

claim: The small-sized genetic similarity clusters are consistent with phylogenetic clustering studies in generalized epidemics in Southern Africa.
source: This is consistent with phylogenetic clustering studies in generalized epidemics in Southern Africa but contrasts with larger clusters typically found in concentrated HIV epidemics in Europe and North America (Grabowski et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion section cites a comparison with other phylogenetic studies.

claim: Most participants in the household survey indicated they had not engaged in transactional sex in the last 12 months.
source: Most participants in the household survey of the Botswana/Ya Tsie trial indicated that they had not engaged in transactional sex in the last 12 months.
evidence: The discussion section reports survey data on sexual behavior.

claim: This suggested that there was a limited contribution of sex workers to the transmission patterns identified in the trial.
source: This suggested that there was a limited contribution of sex workers to the transmission patterns identified in the trial.
evidence: The discussion section interprets survey data on sexual behavior.

claim: The sampling fraction was a relatively small sample (14%) of HIV viral genomes in the trial population.
source: First, viral genomes from an estimated 14% of all people with HIV aged 16–64 years were sampled among participating trial communities. Comparatively, the sampling fraction of phylogenetic studies based on African genomes is commonly under 10% (Grabowski et al., 2018). Although our sampling fraction was a modest improvement over previous studies it is a relatively small sample of HIV viral genomes in the trial population.
evidence: The discussion section acknowledges a limitation regarding sampling fraction.

claim: Most participants with HIV in this trial were virally suppressed, which might have biased the results.
source: Most participants with HIV in this trial were virally suppressed, this might have biased our results in the sense that there might be some differences between the HIV transmission patterns we found and those that exist among viral genetic clusters largely populated by people with unsuppressed virus.
evidence: The discussion section acknowledges a potential source of bias.

claim: The study was based on a relatively representative sample of adults with HIV living in rural and peri-urban villages across Eastern Botswana.
source: Nevertheless, this study was based on a relatively representative sample of adults with HIV living in rural and peri-urban villages across Eastern Botswana.
evidence: The discussion section characterizes the representativeness of the sample.

claim: There was a greater flow of HIV transmissions into intervention communities from control communities than vice versa potentially reducing the observed effect-size of the trial.
source: Moreover, there was a greater flow of HIV transmissions into intervention communities from control communities than vice versa potentially reducing the observed effect-size of the trial, as would transmissions averted by the intervention that were not picked up because the recipient was not in a trial community.
evidence: The discussion section interprets the implications of transmission patterns for trial outcomes.
